reason: The court adopted the s.71 framework under which the Bank first had to consider whether the land was within its acquisition authority.
The quote supports the s.71(2) restriction issue, but the statement is vague and drops the Finance Act acquisition context.
The statement reflects a factual finding on the evidence rather than a legal ratio suitable as a case rule.
The court held this mortgage decree and sale were not nullities, but the statement omits the section 15 Mortgage Act and competent-court/default context.
The court held receivable rent ran from the Rent Act commencement date, not from an agreed date.
The court held the deposit-in-court relief was not available, so the statement reverses the holding.
The substance is supported, but the statement's reference to section (c) of the Rent Act is materially defective.
The court held that transferees taking only undivided shares could not rely on the predecessor's alleged prescription to a specific lot.
The court decided that this particular elucidating amendment did not alter the action, not that plaint amendments generally do not do so.
The succession rule based on the original dedication was expressly adopted as part of the holding.
The statement omits the material qualification that the bequest was in common with succession in turn by seniority.
The quote states a definite rule for exempt temples, while the statement incorrectly says the applicable rule is unspecified.
The abandonment and new tenancy finding is supported, but CPC s.328 was not the provision construed for that standalone tenancy proposition.
The co-owner leasing rule is supported, but it is not a construction of CPC s.328 as claimed in the statute field.
The appellate procedural point is supported, but it is not a rule construing CPC s.328.
The court directly construed the Conciliation Boards timing point and used it to hold the tort claim was not prescribed.
The statement omits the condition that the original and duplicate deed were unavailable, making secondary evidence admissible.
The Day Book point is supported but depends on missing registry materials and use as secondary proof of the lost folio and registration.
The court held the gift deed prevailed by both priority of execution and priority of registration, not execution alone.
The court directly held that principal-agent issues were governed by corresponding English law under section 3 of the Civil Law Ordinance.
The authority finding is supported, but the statement omits that it turned on the contract, evidence, and customary course of this business.
The court found these defendants had pledge authority in the proved Factors Act and business context, not that every such agent in possession has that authority.
The court held Harry Halangoda's beneficial interest was limited to life income and not dominium over the trust capital.
Section 10 permitted disposal within twelve months unless a tenant applied, and the ratio concerned whether an agreement to sell was a disposal.
The presumption was central, but the statement omits the condition that the original will was in the testator's possession and not forthcoming at death.
